cards.title: Six cash-conversion levers that gate bootstrap growth
cards.summary: Model DTC growth as a cash conversion cycle and diagnose which of six levers — CAC, AOV, maintained markup, return rate, sell-through, OpEx — is your current constraint before spending more on ads.
cards.use_when: You are planning next quarter's growth budget and deciding whether to spend more on acquisition or fix margins/inventory/Opex first
steps: Define the cash conversion cycle (CCC) as the time to turn inventory into cash — for a bootstrapped store it is the limiter on how fast you can grow, because you need capital available to fund marketing and the next inventory buy.
Break CCC into six operable levers: CAC, average order value (AOV), maintained markup (MMU), returning-customer rate, 30-day sell-through rate, and operating expenses (OpEx).

For each lever, trace the mechanism: CAC and AOV act mainly through revenue and gross profit; MMU lowers COGS and the stock required to serve the same revenue; return rate adds revenue with little reacquisition cost; sell-through frees cash from inventory without touching P&L; OpEx hits net income 1:1.

Build a simple monthly model with starting inventory, inventory purchase, marketing spend, revenue split new vs. repeat, COGS (shipping, fulfillment, transaction fees), then OpEx, to get net income and ending cash.
Identify the single lever currently most constraining the model and attack it first rather than optimizing everything at once.
Re-run the model after the change and look at the 60/90/180-day cash position, not the first 30 days.
caveats: Mechanisms are explained qualitatively; the numbers in the talk are illustrative model outputs, not benchmarks for your store.
The source assumes purchase orders are sized off lead time or sell-through assumptions — your model must reflect your real supplier terms.
cards.source_name: The Six Bottlenecks in eCommerce Growth.docx

cards.title: Variable vs fixed expense rule: why OpEx cuts hit cash 1:1
cards.summary: The source's core accounting distinction: cutting fixed OpEx improves net income and net cash one-for-one, while cutting variable marketing spend does not.
cards.use_when: You are deciding where to cut to improve cash position without stalling revenue
steps: Separate expenses into fixed (OpEx — staff, software, rent) and variable (marketing, shipping, fees).

Recognize that a dollar removed from fixed OpEx flows directly to net income and net cash; a dollar removed from marketing reduces revenue and COGS too, so the net cash effect is far smaller and can be negative.
Audit OpEx for costs added during past revenue peaks and never removed, especially staffing built for inflated topline.

In the source's example, a brand cutting OpEx from $255k to $119k improved net income by about $6k and net cash by $7k with no change to revenue or gross profit, described as a 4x profitability swing — treat as a model illustration, not a promise.
Pair the cut with a plan for which freed cash goes back into high-ROI reinvestment.
caveats: The '1:1' relationship applies to fixed expenses only; do not assume it for marketing or other variable costs.
Do not cut OpEx that directly generates revenue or retention without modelling the second-order effect.
cards.source_name: The Six Bottlenecks in eCommerce Growth.docx

cards.title: The 60-180 day lag on lever changes
cards.summary: Small financial-lever improvements rarely show up in a 30-day window; the compounding effect lands at 60-180 days in the net cash position.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating whether a CAC, AOV or margin change is working and deciding when to judge it
steps: Expect no visible cash improvement in the first 30 days after a lever change — inventory purchases and cash timing mask it.
Extend the review horizon to 60, 90 and 180 days before declaring a lever successful or dead.

In the source's model, dropping CAC from $65 to $50 kept the business roughly flat in month one but by day 60 produced a 7x swing in monthly profitability and roughly $199k more in ending cash — a model illustration, not a forecast.
Report lever performance to stakeholders against the longer horizon so short-term flatness doesn't kill a working change.
Keep the pre-change baseline model so you can compare period over period rather than month over month.
caveats: The 60-180 day figure is the presenter's observation from his model, not an established benchmark for all stores.
Compounding depends on actually reinvesting the freed cash, not just banking it.
cards.source_name: The Six Bottlenecks in eCommerce Growth.docx

cards.title: Improving AOV without adding fixed cost
cards.summary: Raising AOV lifts revenue and gross profit while fixed marketing and OpEx stay flat, accelerating inventory turnover and shortening the cash cycle.
cards.use_when: You want faster cash turnover without increasing ad spend, e.g. on PDP, bundles or post-purchase upsells
steps: Model the mechanism first: an AOV increase raises new and returning revenue with the same customer count and no added fixed expense, so inventory turns faster and net income improves.

In the source's model, moving AOV from $150 to $180 (about 30%) took net income from $2.6k to $16.3k in month one, and by month three to $175k versus $3.5k in the base case — described as a 10x+ swing in net cash flow, illustrative not guaranteed.
Apply AOV tactics that don't raise COGS proportionally or cannibalize margin: quantity bundles, size/format upsells, threshold-based free shipping, complementary add-ons on the PDP and in cart.
Re-check that the AOV gains don't increase return rate or shipping/fulfillment cost per order enough to eat the gross profit.
Track AOV alongside CCC in your monthly model to confirm the cash effect, not just the revenue effect.
caveats: The specific dollar figures come from the presenter's spreadsheet and assume fixed customer counts and no extra fixed cost.
AOV gains from discounting can lower maintained markup and offset the cash benefit.
cards.source_name: The Six Bottlenecks in eCommerce Growth.docx

cards.title: Maintained markup as an inventory-cash unlock
cards.summary: Raising MMU through supplier negotiation and on-site pricing cuts COGS and the stock needed for the same revenue, freeing cash even when the P&L gain looks modest.
cards.use_when: You are renegotiating supplier terms or repricing core SKUs and want to quantify the cash effect, not just the margin
steps: Understand the dual mechanism: higher MMU lowers COGS, and it lowers the inventory required to service the same revenue level, which is where the real cash unlock sits.

In the source's example, moving MMU from 4 to 4.5 — from slight supplier negotiation plus slight on-site price increases — roughly doubled net cash flow in month three (about $1.5k to $5k) and cut required inventory from $55k to under $50k, moving ending cash from $50k to $62k.
Pursue both sides: negotiate landed cost and make measured price increases on the site, verifying demand elasticity so volume doesn't collapse.
Recompute required inventory at the new margin and release the freed cash into marketing or the next buy rather than leaving it in stock.
Treat MMU gains as compounding with sell-through gains when you cut low-margin SKUs.
caveats: The source notes MMU's P&L gain is smaller than CAC/AOV levers — the argument for it is the inventory cash release.
Price increases can reduce conversion; the source presents 'slight' adjustments, not a formula.
cards.source_name: The Six Bottlenecks in eCommerce Growth.docx

cards.title: Returning-customer rate as the near-zero-CAC profit driver
cards.summary: The source argues returning customers generate 80-90% of net profit because reacquisition costs are minimal, so retention spend raises both net income and cash.
cards.use_when: You are allocating budget between acquisition and retention, or building post-purchase and lifecycle email flows
steps: Decompose total revenue into new-customer and repeat-customer revenue in your model so the repeat share is visible.
Recognize the mechanism: repeat purchases add revenue and gross profit with little or no acquisition cost, so they flow almost directly to net income.

In the source's example, raising the returning-customer share from 25% to 35% via more email and a more considered first-purchase experience moved revenue from $98k to $113k and net income by about $10k, described as 5x on net cash flow — a model illustration.
Invest in the levers that create returns: post-purchase email flows, a better first-purchase experience, and retention programs.
Account for the real cost of retention activity (an agency, a hire) in the model rather than assuming the gain is free.
caveats: The 80-90% of profit from repeat buyers is the presenter's assertion from his modelling, not a measured universal benchmark.
The example assumes no increase in fixed expenses; in practice retention initiatives usually add some cost.
cards.source_name: The Six Bottlenecks in eCommerce Growth.docx

cards.title: Using 30-day sell-through to free trapped cash
cards.summary: Raising 30-day sell-through cuts the next inventory buy, releasing cash tied up in stock without changing revenue or gross profit.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing SKU range and open-to-buy and want to convert dead stock into cash
steps: Define sell-through over a fixed window (the source uses 30 days) as units sold divided by units available, per SKU.
Identify SKUs with weak sell-through and cut them from the range, especially those with poor maintained markup.
Improve purchasing and inventory management so the next PO is sized off actual sell-through and lead time rather than optimistic forecasts.

In the source's example, lifting sell-through from 30% to 40% by trimming poor SKUs and better purchasing unlocked about $220k from inventory and moved ending cash from $50k to $70k — illustrative model output.
Note this lever doesn't change net income or gross profit; its purpose is releasing cash for reinvestment into marketing and future buys.
Re-calculate open-to-buy after every range decision so the freed cash is redeployed deliberately.
caveats: Cutting SKUs can reduce top-line choice and affect conversion; the source pairs the cut with low-MMU SKUs specifically.
The dollar unlocks in the example are model outputs, not benchmarks.
cards.source_name: The Six Bottlenecks in eCommerce Growth.docx

cards.title: The compounding lever strategy: move 2-3 levers at once
cards.summary: Adjusting two to three levers simultaneously — e.g. OpEx, MMU and sell-through — compounds into a much larger net cash position than any single fix.
cards.use_when: You are building a turnaround or growth plan and need to prioritise several financial fixes at once
steps: Start from a base model of a brand with $25k OpEx, 4.0 MMU and 30% 30-day sell-through, as the source does.

Apply three simultaneous changes: cut OpEx from $25k to $19k by right-sizing staff left over from peak revenue; negotiate suppliers and adjust site pricing to move MMU from 4.0 to 4.5; cut weak, low-margin SKUs to raise sell-through.

Track the combined effect: in the source's example net income went from $3.5k to $12.2k per month, net cash flow from $1.7k to $11.2k, and net cash position from $50k to $91k — nearly doubling, without touching CAC, AOV or return rate.
Prioritise levers by how quickly each releases cash: OpEx and sell-through free cash fastest, MMU compounds over longer horizons.
Reinvest the freed cash into the highest-ROI activity, typically marketing, to convert the cash unlock into growth.
Re-run the model before adding more levers so you can see which combinations compound best.
caveats: The doubling result is from the presenter's illustrative model, not a guaranteed outcome.
Running too many changes at once makes attribution difficult; keep a baseline model to isolate effects.
cards.source_name: The Six Bottlenecks in eCommerce Growth.docx

cards.title: Model cash flow monthly, not just net income
cards.summary: A store can be net-income positive while its bank balance falls, because inventory purchases pull cash directly — so model the bank balance as well.
cards.use_when: You are reviewing monthly P&L and wondering why profit isn't showing up as cash, or sizing the next inventory buy
steps: Extend your monthly P&L into a cash view: starting cash, inventory purchase, marketing, revenue, COGS (shipping, fulfillment, transaction fees), OpEx, then net income and ending cash.
Reconcile the difference: a positive net income can still produce a lower bank balance in the same month because the inventory purchase pulls cash out of the account.
Roll the model forward at least 30/60/90 days so inventory build and lead-time purchases are visible in the cash line, not just the P&L.
Size inventory purchases off sell-through and lead time assumptions, then stress-test those assumptions down to see the cash impact.
Watch ending cash, not net income, as the constraint on how fast you can increase marketing and inventory spend.
caveats: This is a simplified monthly model; it omits working capital details like payment terms and supplier deposits.
Sell-through and lead-time assumptions drive the whole model, so verify them against actuals.
cards.source_name: The Six Bottlenecks in eCommerce Growth.docx
